description: Standards, conventions and operational practices for my projects, labs and public portfolio.

books.title: Principles
books.description: Mission, user responsibility, ethics and long-term stewardship

pages.title: Professional Principles
pages.description: Software engineering is valuable when it helps a person do something with less friction, less uncertainty or less risk. A system may be commissioned by an organization and shaped by commercial constraints, but its quality is eventually experienced by the person who has to use it, trust it or recover from its failure.

pages.title: Mission
pages.description: The deepest satisfaction I find in programming is not that a program runs, or that a difficult implementation is complete. It is the moment when work made with thought and care becomes useful in another person's day: a search becomes possible, a repeated task becomes lighter, an answer becomes more reliable, or someone reaches what they needed with less difficulty.

pages.title: Users First
pages.description: A user does not normally want a database, a deployment or a form. The user wants to find a book, submit a request, understand a result, complete a job or recover from a problem. Engineering starts by understanding that goal well enough to reduce its friction without creating avoidable risk.

pages.title: Engineering Ethics
pages.description: Software can save time, reveal information, control access, record decisions and influence what people are able to do. Engineering ethics is therefore not an optional discussion after implementation. It is the discipline of noticing whose interests and risks are affected by a technical choice, then acting honestly and competently.

pages.title: Craftsmanship Without Ego
pages.description: Craftsmanship in software is not devotion to elaborate code or personal style. It is care for correctness, clarity and changeability in proportion to the system's consequences. The work is successful when it serves users and can be responsibly maintained by people who did not write it.

pages.title: Pragmatism Without Negligence
pages.description: Pragmatism means selecting an adequate solution for real constraints: user need, risk, time, cost, skills and operating capacity. It does not mean shipping whatever is fastest regardless of consequences.

pages.title: Long-Term Responsibility
pages.description: When people depend on software, delivery is the beginning of responsibility, not its end. A deployed system needs ownership, observation, maintenance and an eventual path for replacement or retirement.

pages.title: References and Adoption Notes
pages.description: This section begins with a personal mission: build software that creates a useful bridge between people and their everyday goals. The positions in these documents are this playbook's own. The external sources below provide professional and operational guidance that strengthens particular duties and practices; they are not presented as authors of the personal mission.

pages.title: Architecture Standards
pages.description: Architecture guidance for building systems that can be deployed, operated, changed and understood over time. This section documents decision logic and operational consequences, not target-state diagrams detached from delivery.

pages.title: Principles and Tradeoffs
pages.description: This playbook treats architecture as the set of decisions that constrain how a system changes and operates. The aim is not an idealized platform; it is a system whose complexity is justified by real requirements.

pages.title: Boundaries and Service Design
pages.description: System boundaries define ownership of behavior, data, change and failure. Deployable services should follow boundaries that are already understood, not serve as an expensive experiment for finding them.

pages.title: Runtime and Platform Topology
pages.description: Runtime architecture connects software boundaries to deployable units, networks, ingress, secrets, storage and operator responsibilities.

pages.title: State, Reliability and Scale
pages.description: The most consequential architecture choices usually involve data and failure. Stateless application replicas are easy to recreate; durable state and cross-service correctness are not.

pages.title: Time and Timezone Standards
pages.description: Time handling is an architecture concern because it affects data correctness, user trust, audit evidence, scheduling, integrations and incident response. Global systems must distinguish an instant on the timeline from a local civil date/time and from a user's display preference.

pages.title: Delivery and Evolution
pages.description: Architecture must survive change. A topology that works only when deployed by hand or understood by its original author is not a durable production design.

pages.title: References and Adoption Notes
pages.description: This architecture standard uses external guidance as input, then adapts it to small and production-oriented platform contexts. The choice to prefer modular deployment boundaries, require operational consequences in ADRs and introduce complexity only after a demonstrated need is this playbook's convention, not a requirement imposed by the external sources.

pages.title: Architecture Decision Records
pages.description: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) preserve context for choices that affect system boundaries, operations, reliability, security, cost or delivery. They are intentionally short enough to maintain alongside code and infrastructure.

pages.title: ADR-NNNN: Decision Title
pages.description: Describe the requirement, constraint or problem that makes this decision necessary. Include current operating conditions, known scale, reliability, security or cost needs. Avoid describing a solution before the problem.

pages.title: CI/CD Standards
pages.description: Standards for building, validating, publishing and deploying software through repeatable automation with controlled production risk.

pages.title: Pipeline Principles
pages.description: CI/CD should reduce manual uncertainty without granting automation unlimited authority. A useful pipeline makes failures visible early, creates one traceable artifact and makes production change deliberate and reversible.

pages.title: GitHub Actions Workflows
pages.description: GitHub Actions is the default workflow example in this playbook because it is practical for public repositories and portfolio projects. The principles still apply when another CI/CD system is used.

pages.title: Build and Artifacts
pages.description: Artifacts should be reproducible enough to investigate, immutable enough to promote and identifiable enough to roll back. Container images are the primary deployment artifact in this playbook.

pages.title: Releases and Versioning
pages.description: A release is a traceable decision to make a tested artifact available for use, not merely a Git tag or a generated changelog.

pages.title: Deployments and Promotion
pages.description: Deployment automation changes a running environment. Its standard is therefore higher than build automation: it must select a trusted artifact, use scoped authority, verify result and support recovery.

pages.title: Pipeline Operations
pages.description: Delivery automation needs its own operations model: failures, duration, resource consumption and dependency trust affect engineering throughput and production risk.

pages.title: CI/CD Delivery Checklist
pages.description: Use this checklist when introducing delivery automation, releasing an image or changing a production deployment path.

pages.title: References and Adoption Notes
pages.description: The sources below describe platform capabilities or established delivery practices. This playbook converts them into an opinionated but proportional standard: build once, publish an immutable artifact, promote with environment isolation, verify deployments and add governance only where project impact requires it.

books.title: Docker
books.description: Container builds, images and runtime conventions

pages.title: Docker Standards
pages.description: Production-oriented standards for building, publishing and operating containerized workloads consistently across local development, portfolio services and managed deployment platforms.

pages.title: Container Principles
pages.description: Containers make an application portable only when their boundaries are clear: what is in the image, what is supplied at runtime, what is persisted and what must be operated outside the container.

pages.title: Dockerfiles and Builds
pages.description: A production Dockerfile should be predictable to review, efficient enough to build repeatedly and narrow enough that its runtime image contains only what the application needs to execute.

pages.title: Images and Registries
pages.description: Container images are release artifacts. Registry layout, tags, provenance and retention affect deployment safety, rollback and supply-chain trust.

pages.title: Runtime and Process Model
pages.description: A runtime image must behave predictably during startup, health checking, termination, debugging and replacement. These properties matter more in production than squeezing the final few megabytes from an image.

pages.title: Networking and Storage
pages.description: Networks and storage determine whether containerized workloads remain isolated, durable and recoverable. Container packaging does not make persistent data or reachability safe by default.

pages.title: Compose and Local Development
pages.description: Docker Compose is an effective way to express local multi-container dependencies and small deployments. Its value is consistency, not forcing production topology to be identical to a laptop.

pages.title: Orchestration and Production
pages.description: Production container operation combines image discipline with scheduling, networking, secrets, state, rollout behavior and recovery. The orchestrator does not repair an image that lacks runtime clarity.

pages.title: Docker Operational Checklist
pages.description: Use this checklist when adding a containerized service, publishing an image or reviewing a production deployment.

pages.title: References and Adoption Notes
pages.description: These sources define Docker platform behavior or established operating guidance. This playbook adapts them to practical portfolio and production systems. Its decisions to prefer one runtime image per independently deployed capability, use digest-based production promotion and avoid unnecessary orchestration complexity are local conventions rather than requirements of Docker or Kubernetes.

pages.title: GitHub Standards
pages.description: Practical standards for managing repositories, collaboration, delivery automation and security controls on GitHub.

pages.title: Repository Configuration
pages.description: A repository should make ownership, purpose, delivery status and documentation discoverable before someone opens source files or workflow YAML.

pages.title: Branching Strategies
pages.description: Branching strategy is an engineering and release-management decision. Choose the simplest model that supports release, maintenance and audit requirements without introducing unnecessary integration delay.

pages.title: Branches, Commits and Pull Requests
pages.description: The collaboration flow should keep the trusted branch reviewable and releasable while avoiding process that exceeds project risk.

pages.title: Issues, Projects and Releases
pages.description: GitHub planning features should improve discoverability and release traceability, not create duplicate administration for small projects.

pages.title: Actions and Delivery Integration
pages.description: GitHub Actions workflows can validate changes, publish artifacts and deploy environments. A workflow with registry or production access is privileged delivery code and must be reviewed accordingly.

pages.title: Access, Secrets and Security
pages.description: Repository access and automation credentials must reflect what a person or workflow actually needs to do. GitHub is often the first point from which production authority, packages and public source can be altered.

pages.title: Lifecycle and Portfolio Presentation
pages.description: Repositories have a lifecycle: creation, active delivery, publication, maintenance and retirement. A public portfolio repository also communicates engineering judgment to readers who will not know its private context.

pages.title: GitHub Repository Checklist
pages.description: Use this checklist for a new repository, a public portfolio review or a repository that now controls production delivery.

pages.title: References and Adoption Notes
pages.description: These sources describe GitHub platform features or broadly used engineering conventions. This playbook adapts them to repositories that range from public portfolio work to production delivery. Its thresholds for process, preference for concise governance and exact repository taxonomy are local conventions.

pages.title: Infrastructure Standards
pages.description: Standards for organizing, provisioning and operating infrastructure that supports software delivery and production workloads.

pages.title: Principles and Boundaries
pages.description: Infrastructure standards should reduce operational ambiguity. They should not force a small system to mimic a large organization without the same failure, scale or compliance requirements.

pages.title: Topology and Environments
pages.description: Infrastructure topology should describe traffic paths, placement, state, administrative authority and failure domains. A diagram that only names products is insufficient for operation.

pages.title: Networking and Edge
pages.description: Network topology should express which systems may communicate and why. A working connection is not evidence that exposure is safe.

pages.title: Clusters and Orchestration
pages.description: An orchestrator provides placement and reconciliation capabilities. It also creates a control plane, upgrade path, access boundary and recovery burden. Select it for operational requirements rather than portfolio appearance.

pages.title: Storage, Backup and Recovery
pages.description: Durable state is where infrastructure claims become testable. Replicas and containers do not remove data ownership, consistency or restore obligations.

pages.title: Provisioning and Lifecycle
pages.description: Infrastructure should be provisioned so that intended state, authority, changes and recovery are reviewable. Automation is useful when it reduces drift and risk, not when it obscures who can change production.

pages.title: Observability and Operations
pages.description: Infrastructure operation requires enough telemetry and access to distinguish application failure from network, node, storage, control-plane or provider failure. Collecting signals without an operator decision path is not operability.

pages.title: Reliability, Cost and Maturity
pages.description: Infrastructure maturity is not measured by the number of technologies in use. It is measured by whether risk, reliability, recovery, cost and ownership are understood for the system being operated.

pages.title: Infrastructure Checklist
pages.description: Use this checklist when creating, reviewing, promoting or materially changing infrastructure. Apply depth proportional to user impact and data value.

pages.title: References
pages.description: This section uses official platform and reliability guidance to ground operational behavior. The specific topology tiers, checklist structure and small-platform recommendations are local standards adapted for this playbook, not mandates from the cited sources.

pages.title: Naming Standards
pages.description: Consistent names reduce mistakes in deployment, incident response and automation. This section defines stable naming rules for repositories, delivery artifacts, runtime resources and operational telemetry.

pages.title: Core Naming Syntax
pages.description: This document defines the shared vocabulary. Domain-specific documents may tighten these rules when a platform imposes additional syntax.

pages.title: Source Control and Artifacts
pages.description: These conventions cover source repositories and the immutable artifacts that move through the delivery pipeline.

pages.title: Automation and Environments
pages.description: Automation names need to work both in configuration syntax and in the operator-facing CI/CD interface.

pages.title: Runtime and Infrastructure Resources
pages.description: Runtime names appear in deployment commands, routing, secret grants and recovery procedures. Favor stable service purpose over implementation detail.

pages.title: Telemetry and Operations
pages.description: A resource name is only useful if it remains recognizable in metrics, logs, traces and alerts. Telemetry SHOULD preserve the same system and component vocabulary used by deployments.

pages.title: References and Adoption Notes
pages.description: This playbook deliberately applies a conservative shared naming subset across systems. External documents below provide platform constraints or established semantic vocabulary. Rules such as the single environment vocabulary, <system>-<component> ordering and Docker tag promotion policy are local standards adopted here for operational consistency; they are not claimed as requirements of those external projects.

pages.title: Observability Standards
pages.description: Standards for producing, collecting and using telemetry to operate software and infrastructure safely in production.

pages.title: Principles and Signal Model
pages.description: Observability should help answer: what is failing, who is affected, what changed, why it is happening and which recovery action is safe.

pages.title: Logging and Correlation
pages.description: Logs should preserve evidence needed for diagnosis without becoming an uncontrolled copy of application data or credentials.

pages.title: Metrics, SLOs and Alerts
pages.description: Metrics are best for rates, trends, saturation and objective evaluation. Alerts should be derived from conditions where an operator can reduce impact or prevent an imminent failure.

pages.title: Tracing and OpenTelemetry
pages.description: Tracing is valuable when a request crosses service, queue or provider boundaries and operators need to understand where time or failure is spent. It is not automatically required for a small single-service workload.

pages.title: Dashboards and Visualization
pages.description: Dashboards should guide an operator from service impact to likely causes and support routine capacity or release review. A wall of unrelated graphs slows incident response.

pages.title: Platform and Runtime Monitoring
pages.description: Operational visibility must cover both the behavior users depend on and the runtime layers that explain failure. Container orchestration changes which infrastructure signals matter; it does not remove application instrumentation.

pages.title: Pipelines, Storage and Cost
pages.description: An observability pipeline is production infrastructure. If it fails silently, operators may lose evidence at the same time a workload fails.

pages.title: Diagnostics and Incident Workflows
pages.description: Observability proves its value during change, degradation and incidents. Diagnostics should direct investigation from symptom to cause without random production mutation.

pages.title: Observability Checklist
pages.description: Use this checklist for a new deployed service, a monitoring stack change or a production readiness review.

pages.title: References
pages.description: This section uses primary operational and tool documentation for signal, query, correlation and alerting behavior. The particular document split, baseline stack examples and maturity decisions are local playbook conventions, not mandatory external frameworks.

pages.title: Repository Standards
pages.description: Standards for choosing repository boundaries, organizing content and governing project lifecycles across software, infrastructure, platform work and public portfolio material.

pages.title: Principles and Boundaries
pages.description: Repository boundaries influence who can change a system, how it is released, what it exposes publicly and how easily an operator can discover the relevant documentation during a problem.

pages.title: Monorepo and Multirepo
pages.description: Monorepo versus multirepo is an ownership and change-management decision, not a proxy for architectural sophistication. Either model can support monoliths, microservices, infrastructure and platform delivery.

pages.title: Repository Types
pages.description: A clear repository taxonomy improves discovery and prevents fundamentally different assets from being governed as if they share the same lifecycle.

pages.title: Structure and Documentation
pages.description: Repository structure should help a maintainer find code, delivery controls, decisions and operations without learning a unique layout for every project.

pages.title: Visibility and Portfolio
pages.description: Repository visibility changes who can see source, history, workflows, issues, artifacts and documentation. Treat visibility as part of repository design, not a last-minute GitHub setting.

pages.title: Ownership and Lifecycle
pages.description: A repository with no owner eventually accumulates broken workflows, outdated dependencies, unanswered security findings and unclear production authority. Ownership can be lightweight, but it must be explicit.

pages.title: Repository Checklist
pages.description: Use this checklist when creating a repository, making it public, adding production responsibility or retiring it.

pages.title: References and Adoption Notes
pages.description: The sources below define GitHub platform behavior or provide concrete experience with repository and decision-management models. This playbook adapts them into a proportional repository standard. Its repository taxonomy, default boundaries and portfolio curation rules are local conventions rather than universal requirements.

pages.title: Operational Runbooks
pages.description: Repeatable procedures for investigating, mitigating and recovering production services and their supporting platform infrastructure.

pages.title: Principles and Readiness
pages.description: Runbooks are operating code written for a human or an automation system. A procedure that is unclear, unsafe or obsolete during failure increases outage duration and can create a second incident.

pages.title: Incident Response and Communication
pages.description: Incident response should minimize user impact while preserving enough information to restore service safely and prevent repeat failure.

pages.title: Troubleshooting Methodology
pages.description: Troubleshooting is a controlled reduction of uncertainty. The goal is not to try commands until the symptom disappears; it is to identify the affected boundary and select a safe corrective action.

pages.title: Deployment Rollback and Service Recovery
pages.description: Use this runbook when a service degrades after a deployment or when a known good artifact can restore behavior. Rollback reverses application release state; it does not automatically reverse data migrations or infrastructure changes.

pages.title: Containers and Orchestration
pages.description: Use this runbook when workload failure appears at container, node or orchestrator level. Diagnose user impact and deployment state before restarting or rescheduling processes.

pages.title: Network, Edge, DNS and TLS
pages.description: Use this runbook when a service is healthy internally but unreachable, fails TLS validation or cannot communicate through expected network paths.

pages.title: Data and Infrastructure Recovery
pages.description: Stateful and infrastructure recovery procedures carry higher risk than application restart or image rollback. Stop and escalate when the data version, recovery target or destructive consequence is unclear.

pages.title: Security and Delivery Recovery
pages.description: Operational incidents frequently intersect with credentials, delivery authority or artifact trust. Contain active security risk before optimizing availability when a compromised path could continue causing harm.

pages.title: Commands and Safe Execution
pages.description: Commands in runbooks are examples that must be adapted to the known environment, ownership boundary and access policy. Begin with read-only inspection; mark mutating actions explicitly in incident notes.

pages.title: Templates and Checklists
pages.description: These templates are intentionally concise. Extend them for a specific service when state, compliance, user communication or platform complexity requires it.

pages.title: References
pages.description: This section uses official reliability, operations and platform documentation to establish safe operational practices. Severity labels, document layout, example commands and lightweight workflows are local conventions adapted for this playbook.

pages.title: Security Standards
pages.description: Practical controls for protecting source code, delivery pipelines, credentials and containerized workloads without turning small engineering projects into a compliance program.

pages.title: Secrets and Credentials
pages.description: Secrets include API tokens, passwords, private keys, signing keys, connection strings containing credentials, webhook secrets and cloud access material. Their operational value is access, so they require lifecycle management rather than careful file naming alone.

pages.title: Identity and Access
pages.description: Access design should make normal work easy while making broad or unexplained access unusual. A useful least-privilege policy answers who or what needs access, to which environment, for which action and for how long.

pages.title: CI/CD and Automation Security
pages.description: Delivery pipelines sit between source code and production authority. Treat a workflow that can publish an image or deploy production as privileged code.

pages.title: Containers and Supply Chain
pages.description: Container security has two parts: build trustworthy artifacts and run them with limited authority. A minimal image is useful, but it is not a substitute for provenance, patching and runtime isolation.

pages.title: Repository and Data Hygiene
pages.description: Security failures in engineering repositories are often mundane: a committed .env file, a debug log containing a token, a production export uploaded as a demo fixture or a portfolio screenshot showing internal infrastructure.

pages.title: Security Incident Response
pages.description: This procedure is intentionally lightweight. It is meant to make the first hour of a likely credential or access incident predictable for small and mid-sized engineering workloads.

pages.title: Security Baseline Checklist
pages.description: Use this checklist when creating a project, enabling CI/CD, preparing a public portfolio release or reviewing a persistent deployment. Not every advanced item is required; every unchecked baseline item needs remediation or an explicit exception.

pages.title: References and Adoption Notes
pages.description: The sources below supply authoritative platform behavior or widely used security guidance. This playbook adapts them into a practical baseline for containerized projects, automation pipelines and public portfolio workloads. Its control levels, naming examples and recommended minimum implementation are local conventions, not certification claims.
